ROCHESTER, Minn., and PHOENIX — A Mayo Clinic study published in the Journal of Neuro-Oncology suggests that analyzing DNA in cerebrospinal fluid could provide another source of information when MRI cannot provide a clear brain tumor diagnosis or obtaining tissue through biopsy is difficult or potentially unsafe.
The study included 76 patients facing one of three challenging clinical scenarios:
An abnormality in the brain or spinal cord without a diagnosis;
Imaging changes that could reflect either tumor growth or treatment effects; or
Suspected leptomeningeal disease, in which cancer spreads to the membranes and fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
The investigation detected tumor-associated DNA in 20 patients (26%). For those patients, the findings provided another piece of evidence that clinicians could consider alongside imaging, pathology and the patient's overall clinical picture.
Why can MRI and tissue biopsy leave unanswered questions in brain tumor care?
MRI and tissue biopsy remain essential for diagnosing and monitoring cancers involving the brain and spinal cord. But each has limitations.
Changes on an MRI can often look similar whether they are caused by cancer, inflammation or the effects of treatment. In other cases, a lesion's location may make obtaining tissue through biopsy difficult or unsafe.
Researchers are increasingly studying whether tumor-related material released into body fluids can provide another source of information. A liquid biopsy looks for material such as tumor DNA in a body fluid rather than in a tissue sample. Most liquid biopsies use blood.
For brain tumors, however, the blood-brain barrier — a protective boundary that controls what passes between the bloodstream and the brain — can limit how much tumor DNA reaches the bloodstream, making it difficult to detect.
Mayo Clinic researchers are therefore studying cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, the clear fluid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord. Tumor cells can release small DNA fragments into this fluid. These fragments, known as cell-free DNA, may contain genetic changes associated with a tumor.
Terry Burns, M.D., Ph.D.
CSF can be collected through a lumbar puncture, also known as a spinal tap, in which a thin needle is inserted into the lower back. Researchers then analyze the DNA fragments in the sample for changes in individual genes and broader DNA patterns associated with tumors.
"In some cases, this CSF DNA approach has provided important diagnostic information when obtaining tissue safely was not an option," says Terry Burns, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurosurgeon and senior author of the study.
What did Mayo Clinic researchers find in CSF?
Patients in this study represented three clinical groups:
35 had a brain or spinal cord abnormality whose cause was uncertain;
21 had imaging changes that could represent either tumor progression or treatment-related effects; and
20 were being evaluated for leptomeningeal disease
Across the 76 patients, the analysis found signs of tumor DNA in 20 patients. In 29 patients, the samples contained enough DNA for analysis, but no signs of tumor DNA were detected. The remaining 27 samples did not contain enough usable DNA to complete the analysis.
A negative result did not rule out cancer. The amount of tumor DNA in CSF can vary, and some samples may contain too little tumor DNA for the analysis to detect. Researchers are working to improve the analysis of samples containing very small amounts of DNA.
How could CSF DNA testing inform brain tumor care?
Analyzing cell-free DNA in CSF could provide more than a sign that tumor material is present. The DNA fragments may also contain information about a tumor's genetic features. In the future, that information could help care teams identify clinical trials or treatments that target specific genetic changes.
The test used in this study remains investigational. When it can be obtained safely, tumor tissue remains the gold standard for making a definitive diagnosis. Researchers are working to determine which patients may benefit most from CSF DNA analysis and when the approach could add useful information to imaging, pathology and other established methods.
Cecile Riviere-Cazaux
"Our goal is for CSF cell-free DNA testing to provide patients and their care teams with diagnostic insights when answers may otherwise be difficult to obtain," says Cecile Riviere-Cazaux, a Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine student in Rochester and co-first author of the study. "As we gain more experience, we hope it will also help connect patients with clinical trials and personalized treatment options."
Mayo Clinic researchers are now working to improve the analysis of samples containing very small amounts of tumor DNA and to determine how changes in DNA and other biomarkers over time could help show whether a tumor is responding to treatment.

DEAR MAYO CLINIC: I've always heard that women should begin getting mammograms at a certain age, but now I'm hearing that breast cancer screening can be based on a person's individual risk. How do healthcare professionals determine when and how someone should be screened? And are there newer screening options available for people at higher risk?
ANSWER: Breast cancer screening isn't necessarily one-size-fits-all. While there are general recommendations for when women should begin screening, healthcare professionals also evaluate each patient in context. For women at average risk, screening mammograms generally begin around age 40 and may be recommended every year or every other year. But age is only one part of the picture. Your personal and family history, breast density, and other risk factors can help your healthcare team develop a screening plan based on your individual risk.
Family history is an important part of that assessment. During a routine health visit, your healthcare team may ask whether a mother, sister, aunt or grandparent has had breast cancer. Having a first-degree relative, such as a mother or sister, with breast cancer may lead to a recommendation to meet with a genetic counselor. A genetic counselor reviews your family history, creates a family tree and completes a risk assessment. Based on that information, genetic testing may be offered. Talk openly with family members about their health history. If a relative has had breast cancer, find out when they were diagnosed, the type of breast cancer they had and the treatments they received. This information can be helpful to your healthcare team.
A person's breast cancer risk depends on more than genetics alone. Inherited genetic factors account for only about 5% to 10% of breast cancers. Other factors healthcare professionals may consider include:
Age.
Age when menstrual periods began.
Age at menopause.
Whether you've had children.
Whether you've breastfed.
Alcohol use.
Smoking.
Obesity.
Together, these factors can give your healthcare team a more complete picture of your breast cancer risk.
A person's breast density also can help guide screening decisions. Breast density is grouped into four categories:
Category A: Mostly fatty tissue.
Category B: A mixture of fibroglandular and fatty tissue.
Category C: Moderately dense tissue.
Category D: Extremely dense tissue.
Dense breast tissue is important for two reasons. First, the denser the breast tissue, the more difficult it can be to see through the tissue on a mammogram. Second, glandular and fibrous connective tissue can be more susceptible to breast cancer. Younger women and women with thinner builds may tend to have denser breast tissue, although breast density varies from person to person.
Having dense breasts doesn't necessarily mean you need additional imaging. Your healthcare team will consider breast density along with your other risk factors. For some people, particularly those at higher risk, supplemental screening may include breast MRI, molecular breast imaging or contrast-enhanced mammography.
Advances in imaging also are improving how breast tissue can be evaluated. Three-dimensional mammography, also called digital tomosynthesis, adds a third dimension to traditional two-dimensional mammography. This allows breast radiologists to examine breast tissue in greater detail and look for findings such as calcifications or areas that may be difficult to see. Artificial intelligence also is increasingly being used in modeling and detection to identify tissue patterns that may help healthcare professionals evaluate changes in breast tissue.
Better imaging also may help healthcare teams avoid unnecessary procedures. In the past, a questionable area seen on a two-dimensional mammogram might have led to a fine-needle aspiration, biopsy or lumpectomy to determine whether cancer was present. With improvements in imaging and detection, healthcare professionals may sometimes be able to monitor an area with follow-up imaging, such as another scan in six months, to determine whether it remains stable rather than immediately performing a procedure.
Most importantly, remember that your screening plan may look different from someone else's. A friend with dense breasts may be advised to have additional imaging, for example, but that doesn't necessarily mean you need the same screening. Your healthcare team can consider your age, family history, breast density and other risk factors together to determine which screening approach is appropriate for you.
Graham King, M.D., Menopause and Breast Specialist, Family Medicine, Mayo Clinic Health System, Mankato, Minnesota

ROCHESTER, Minn. — An investigational vaccine helped the immune system recognize and respond to mutations that drive most pancreatic cancers, according to results from a randomized phase 2 clinical trial led by Mayo Clinic researchers. The findings, published in Nature Medicine, will help researchers design a larger phase 3 clinical trial.
Nearly every patient evaluated after receiving the vaccine developed an immune response against mutated KRAS, a gene that plays a major role in pancreatic cancer. Mayo Clinic researchers also found that patients with stronger immune responses tended to remain free of disease longer.
"Historically, pancreatic cancer has been very difficult to treat with immunotherapy," says Ben George, M.B.B.S, M.D., a Mayo Clinic medical oncologist and lead author of the study. "What is encouraging is that we were able to generate a strong immune response against KRAS mutations in nearly every patient we evaluated. In an exploratory analysis, patients with greater immune responses to the vaccine appeared protected with longer disease-free survival times.”
Teaching the immune system what to attack
Pancreatic cancer has a high risk of returning even after surgery and chemotherapy. Researchers have been looking for new ways to find and destroy cancer cells that may remain in the body after treatment.
KRAS offers one possible target.
Mutations in the KRAS gene are found in about 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas, the most common type of pancreatic cancer. These mutations help cancer cells grow and survive.
The investigational vaccine targets seven of the most common KRAS mutations. It is designed to travel to the lymph nodes, where many immune responses begin. There, the vaccine helps T cells — which are immune cells that can recognize and attack altered cells — to identify cancer cells with mutated KRAS.
Unlike some cancer vaccines made specifically for an individual patient, this vaccine is "off the shelf" and designed for patients whose tumors have one of the KRAS mutations it targets.
The study included 144 patients with stage 1-3 KRAS-mutated pancreatic cancer. All had undergone surgery and chemotherapy and had no cancer visible on imaging when they entered the trial.
Researchers randomly assigned 96 patients to receive the vaccine and 48 to observation.
Strong immune response, but more study is needed
The trial did not meet its primary goal of showing an improvement in disease-free survival across the full study population.
Median disease-free survival, or the length of time patients lived without their cancer returning, was 23.8 months for patients who received the vaccine and 21.2 months for those in the observation group. The difference was not statistically significant.
Researchers found other signals that warrant further study.
Of the 90 patients who received the vaccine and could be evaluated for immune response, 89, or 98.9%, developed increased T-cell responses against mutated KRAS.
Researchers also found an association between the strength of the immune response and how long patients remained free of disease. More than 8 in 10 patients who were able to be evaluated developed a KRAS-specific T-cell response that was more than 9 times greater than before vaccination. Patients who reached that level had longer disease-free survival than those who did not.
"The immune response is an important signal that helps us understand what is happening biologically and gives us important information for the next trial," Dr. George says.
Clues about who may benefit
Researchers also found clues that may help predict which patients are more likely to benefit from the vaccine.
One clue involved circulating tumor DNA, or ctDNA. These are small pieces of DNA released by cancer cells into the bloodstream. Detecting ctDNA after cancer treatment can be a sign that cancer remains in the body even when it cannot be seen on imaging.
In a planned analysis, patients who did not have detectable ctDNA at the start of the study showed a signal of longer disease-free survival with the vaccine compared with observation.
Researchers saw another difference based on whether patients had previously received radiation therapy.
Patients who had received radiation had fewer lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell important to the immune system. They also developed weaker KRAS-specific immune responses after receiving the vaccine. Among patients who had not received radiation, researchers saw a signal of longer disease-free survival with the vaccine.
These findings do not establish which patients will benefit from the vaccine. They do, however, give researchers information to test in a larger trial.
"One of the most useful things we can learn from a phase 2 trial is why patients may respond differently," Dr. George says. "We can take those lessons and design the next study to better answer the question that matters most: Can this approach help patients live longer without their pancreatic cancer returning?"
Building an immune response against cancer
Researchers found that the vaccine activated two important types of T cells, known as CD4 and CD8 T cells. It also produced immune responses against several KRAS mutations.
In a small group of patients, researchers observed another potentially important effect. After vaccination, the immune system began recognizing other cancer-related targets that were not included in the vaccine, a phenomenon researchers call antigen spreading.
The immune response also persisted over time. Among patients who could be evaluated at least 46 weeks after the start of the study, 95.5% still had a detectable KRAS-specific T-cell response.
Researchers say longer follow-up and a larger study are needed. Overall survival results are not yet available, and some findings linking immune response with disease-free survival came from exploratory analyses.
A phase 3 clinical trial is planned to further study whether the vaccine can delay or prevent pancreatic cancer from returning.
"We've shown that we can teach the immune system to recognize these KRAS mutations," Dr. George says. "The next step is finding out whether doing that can change the course of the disease for patients."

The post AI tool may support dermatologists in assessing skin lesions for cancer risk appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> ROCHESTER, Minn. — Mayo Clinic researchers have found that an artificial intelligence (AI) tool may provide dermatologists with additional information to help assess whether skin lesions are cancerous and inform their clinical decisions about whether to biopsy or monitor them, according to a study published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings.
The tool, called Dermoscopy Explainable Intelligence (DEXI), is part of an advanced imaging system that dermatologists use to capture and track skin lesions over time. DEXI assigns lesions a score from 0.0 to 10.0 based on image characteristics associated with cancer risk. It also identifies features — such as asymmetry, border and color — that contribute to the score, providing dermatologists with additional information they can consider alongside their clinical evaluation.
Researchers evaluated DEXI scores for skin lesions with known diagnoses. Using a threshold of 3.0 — meaning a score of 3.0 or higher was considered positive for potential skin cancer — DEXI correctly identified 93.4% of cancerous lesions and 75% of noncancerous lesions.
Left: The image is of a non-cancerous skin lesion with a low-risk DEXI score of 1.2 and reassuring features (asymmetry, border, color and diameter) that help inform physicians that it should be monitored. Right: The image of an invasive melanoma with a high-risk DEXI score of 8.9 and features (asymmetry, border, color and diameter) that help inform physicians that it should be biopsied.
"Prior to the study, I would review a patient's DEXI score, but I wouldn't know exactly what to do with the number," says Jenny Link, M.D., dermatologist at Mayo Clinic and the study's lead author. "Now I can confidently use the score as another piece of data to inform my clinical judgment on whether I recommend a biopsy or monitoring."
Study evaluates DEXI's clinical use
DEXI is a deep-learning tool trained on more than 66,000 annotated dermoscopy images. In addition to assigning a cancer risk score, the tool uses explainable AI to indicate which image features contributed to its score.
The retrospective study included 178 patients who underwent total-body photography, sequential digital dermoscopy imaging and subsequent biopsy of one or more skin lesions.
Researchers analyzed 261 lesions with both a DEXI score and a diagnosis confirmed by tissue examination. They compared scores for noncancerous and cancerous lesions and further separated cancerous lesions into melanoma and nonmelanoma skin cancers.
The average DEXI score was 2.5 for noncancerous lesions, compared with 7.8 for nonmelanoma skin cancers and 6.0 for melanomas. Cancerous lesions had significantly higher DEXI scores than noncancerous lesions. Based on these findings, researchers identified 3.0 as a potential threshold that could help inform clinicians' decisions about monitoring or biopsy.
"We identified 3.0 as a potential DEXI score threshold that could provide useful information when dermatologists are considering whether to monitor a lesion or perform a biopsy," says Dr. Link.
The researchers also identified limitations. DEXI does not account for patient-specific factors, such as age, medications and history of melanoma. The tool was also less effective at evaluating severely atypical nevi, or skin moles, and early evolving melanomas.
"Our study demonstrated that DEXI is a useful and valuable tool to support clinicians as they evaluate cancerous and noncancerous skin lesions, but it should not be used in isolation. The score must be interpreted alongside clinical findings and patient-specific factors, and the tool requires further validation and refinement," says Dr. Link.

The post Montana woman’s rare chest tumor calls for integrated surgical care appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Tanya and her husband, Peter, on vacation in Malta about a year after her cancer surgery.
When Tanya's annual physical showed high cholesterol for the second year in a row, the 55-year-old decided it was time for a closer look at her health.
A vegetarian since childhood, Tanya leads an active life filled with travel and adventure. But she also has a family history of heart disease. After talking with her primary care doctor, she chose to undergo comprehensive screening, including a CT scan of her chest.
"The morning of my exams, I said to my husband, 'I can't believe I am doing this. I'm perfectly healthy, right?'" Tanya says.
That afternoon, Tanya was at home in rural Montana when she went online to check her results. She was relieved to see no calcified plaque in her coronary arteries. Then she read something she wasn't expecting.
"Right there, it said, 'a large mass in the chest measuring approximately 15 centimeters.' I was shocked," Tanya says.
She immediately called her doctor.
The next day, Tanya underwent additional CT imaging at her local hospital and met with a pulmonologist. The mass was close to structures surrounding her heart and right lung and would likely require surgery. But Tanya still didn't know what it was.
Her husband, Peter, began searching for a thoracic team with experience treating complex chest tumors. Before the couple even made it home that day, he called Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota.
"It all happened so fast," Tanya says. "Within a few days of finding out I had this massive tumor, I was a patient at Mayo Clinic."
A diagnosis and an integrated care plan
In April 2025, Tanya met Dr. Janani Reisenauer, a Mayo Clinic thoracic surgeon and interventional pulmonologist.
Tanya learned that the mass was a thymoma, a rare tumor that develops in the thymus, a small organ in the area between the lungs and near the heart.
"What made Tanya's case unusual was the sheer size of the tumor and how extensively it involved the structures around her heart and chest," says Dr. Reisenauer.
The cancerous tumor measured the size of a large grapefruit and involved several critical cardiovascular structures in Tanya's chest, including the inferior vena cava, right ventricle, ascending aorta and superior vena cava. It was also compressing her right lung.
Treating it would require expertise from several specialties. Tanya's Mayo Clinic care team included specialists in thoracic surgery, thoracic medical oncology and cardiovascular surgery.
Before surgery, the team recommended chemotherapy in hopes of shrinking the tumor away from critical structures. Tanya met Dr. Aaron Mansfield, a Mayo Clinic thoracic medical oncologist.
"That's when I realized I had cancer. I had to ask him again, 'Do I really have cancer?'" Tanya says. "He was so kind to explain everything that I felt ready and at ease."
But there was something Tanya wanted Dr. Mansfield to know.
"I told him that I had my son's college graduation in two weeks," Tanya says. "Not only did I need to attend, but my family needed to see me happy and confident that I would be OK."
Dr. Mansfield coordinated with Tanya's doctors in Montana so that she could receive chemotherapy close to home and begin treatment after her son's graduation.
"He worked around a life event that was important to me," Tanya says. "It made me feel seen as a person."
Tanya received chemotherapy infusions every three weeks for about three months. Then, she returned to Mayo Clinic for imaging. The tumor had shrunk slightly, but it remained close to her heart and major blood vessels.
Tanya and her husband, Peter, rode a hot air balloon in East Africa as part of their journey to see gorillas in Rwanda.
Two surgical teams remove a complex tumor
Because of the tumor's proximity to major cardiovascular structures, Dr. Reisenauer partnered with Mayo Clinic cardiovascular surgeons to plan Tanya's operation.
On July 28, the team performed a complete thymectomy, removing Tanya's thymus and tumor.
Reaching such a large tumor required extensive access to Tanya's chest. The surgeons made an incision through part of her breastbone and across the right side of her chest, an approach known as a right hemi-clamshell incision.
"It’s a little like seeing beneath the surface to understand how all the components fit together," says Dr. Reisenauer. "By visualizing the anatomy and the relationship between structures, we can better understand what can be safely separated and plan the procedure more precisely."
During the six-hour operation, the surgeons carefully separated the tumor from critical structures, including the right side of Tanya's heart, the superior vena cava and the phrenic nerve, which controls the movement of the diaphragm and plays an important role in breathing.
"The challenge was removing the large tumor in its entirety, without violating the tumor, which we know is a high risk for recurrence," explains Dr. Reisenauer.
Despite the large incision required to reach the tumor, Dr. Reissenauer says the surgeons applied principles of minimally invasive surgery where possible, with the goals of reducing complications, shortening Tanya's hospital stay and helping her recover more quickly.
For Tanya, one of the first signs that the operation went well came from Peter.
"My husband said Dr. Reisenauer had a huge smile when she came to see him," Tanya says. "She told him, 'You're going on that gorilla trek in November.'"
Back to adventure
Tanya and her husband, Peter, went on a safari in East Africa about four months after her cancer surgery.
Tanya recalls waking up after surgery feeling surprisingly well.
"What should have been one of the hardest recoveries of my life was easy because of the excellent care I received," she says.
The surgical team had successfully removed the entire tumor without extra interventions or complications. Within a week, Tanya was walking as many as 5,000 steps a day. Within five weeks, she returned to regular exercise.
And the trip Dr. Reisenauer had remembered was getting closer.
"The fact that she remembered my gorilla trek showed me how much she cared about me as a person," Tanya says.
In November 2025, just months after surgery, Tanya and Peter traveled to Rwanda. At an elevation of 8,000 feet, they trekked through the mountainous jungle in search of gorillas.
"It was remarkable," Tanya says. "Not just the trek, but my experience at Mayo Clinic."
For Tanya, integrated care meant more than removing a complex tumor. It returned her to the adventures that matter to her.

JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — People who develop pancreatic cancer experience measurable changes in body composition years before diagnosis that differ from those seen in similar individuals without cancer, according to a Mayo Clinic study led by former Mayo Clinic research fellow, Aleksander Bogdanski and published in Pancreatology.
Pancreatic cancer remains one of the deadliest cancers, largely because most patients are diagnosed after the disease has already spread. Current surveillance programs focus primarily on people with inherited genetic risk or strong family histories, yet most pancreatic cancers occur outside those high-risk groups.
Researchers found that patients who developed pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common type of pancreatic cancer, experienced steeper declines in visceral and subcutaneous fat over the three years before diagnosis compared with matched controls. The findings suggest that routinely acquired CT scans may capture physiological changes associated with pancreatic cancer before it is clinically detected. To the researchers' knowledge, this is the largest controlled study to examine prediagnostic body composition trajectories in patients who later developed pancreatic cancer.
The study analyzed abdominal CT scans from 1,825 patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and 3,650 matched controls from Mayo Clinic sites in Arizona, Florida and Minnesota. Using an artificial intelligence-based body composition tool, researchers measured changes in skeletal muscle, subcutaneous fat and visceral fat over time.
"Pancreatic cancer often develops silently, making early detection extremely challenging," says Yan Bi, M.D., Ph.D., a gastroenterologist at Mayo Clinic and senior author of the study. "These findings suggest that routine CT scans may capture physiological changes associated with pancreatic cancer before patients are diagnosed."
Compared with controls, patients who developed pancreatic cancer experienced significantly steeper declines in both subcutaneous and visceral fat during the three years before diagnosis. Differences in muscle mass were most apparent during the final 12 months before diagnosis.
"Our study shows that body composition changes associated with pancreatic cancer are detectable on routine CT scans and differ from the changes observed in similar patients without cancer," says Michael Wallace, M.D., a Mayo Clinic gastroenterologist and corresponding author of the study. "To our knowledge, this is the largest controlled study to evaluate these prediagnostic body composition trajectories and one of the first to assess whether they can help distinguish patients who go on to develop pancreatic cancer from those who do not."
Building toward earlier pancreatic cancer risk detection
Researchers also evaluated whether longitudinal changes in muscle and fat measurements could distinguish patients who later developed pancreatic cancer from matched controls. The body composition measures demonstrated moderate discriminatory ability, suggesting they may provide additional information for future risk assessment strategies.
The researchers are working on developing algorithms that incorporate body composition measures along with other routinely collected clinical factors and imaging biomarkers to identify patients at increased risk.

DEAR MAYO CLINIC: There's so much information about breast cancer in women. But I was wondering, do men get breast cancer, and if they do, how is it diagnosed and treated?
ANSWER: Men do get breast cancer — more than 2,500 men in the U.S. are diagnosed with this cancer every year. While accounting for only about 1% of total breast cancers in the U.S., there are some countries in which male breast cancer is more common. As in females, the most common breast cancer in males is ductal carcinoma — about 90% of males are diagnosed with this type of cancer.
What are the symptoms of breast cancer in men?
A lump is the most common symptom of male breast cancer, but there also can be discharge from the nipple or pain in the breast area. A breast lump in males feels much as it does in women — it's usually firmer than the surrounding tissue and may have irregular edges. In men, because they have less breast tissue, the lump is often close to the nipple.
Since breast cancer screenings, such as mammograms and breast exams, aren't typically recommended for men, they usually find a lump on their own. If men notice an unusual lump, experience nipple discharge, or chest or breast discomfort, they should seek medical attention promptly to determine the cause.
Who is at risk for male breast cancer?
The risk for breast cancer in males increases with age and is more common in those who have a family history of breast cancer, especially male breast cancer. Some genetic mutations such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, also are known risk factors. Those with Klinefelter syndrome, a rare condition that occurs when males have an extra X chromosome, also are at higher risk.
Some medical treatments also can put men at greater risk, such as chest wall radiation, sometimes given to treat lymphoma. Some testicular and liver abnormalities that affect hormone levels also increase the risk for male breast cancer.
When should men seek medical care for breast changes?
For men experiencing symptoms, the first step is breast imaging, usually a mammogram and an ultrasound, and sometimes a breast MRI. If the findings of the exam and imaging are concerning, a biopsy will be ordered.
Breast cancer in men is staged the same as in women — from 0 to 4. If detected at stage 0 before the cancer becomes invasive, nearly all patients will be cured. However, if cancer is detected at stage 4, that means it has spread to other parts of the body, and it usually can be treated but not completely eliminated.
Female breast cancers are more often detected at stage 0 and 1, while a higher proportion of male breast cancers are found at stages 2, 3 and 4. When detected at the same stage, the prognosis for breast cancer in a male is no worse than that of breast cancer in a female. However, male breast cancers are more often diagnosed after they have already grown quite large in the breast, spread to lymph nodes under the arm or elsewhere in the body.
If men are diagnosed with stage 0 to 3 cancer, surgery will be part of the treatment plan, while at stage 4, treatments will primarily use medications to fight the cancer throughout the body.
For men requiring surgery, a mastectomy, or the entire removal of the breast tissue, is a common choice. But some men also choose lumpectomy —removal of only part of the breast.
Chemotherapy, endocrine therapy and radiation decisions for men are largely based on evidence from women with breast cancer. However, the Translational Breast Cancer Research Consortium is enrolling men in the ETHAN trial, designed specifically for men. In the ETHAN trial, men who were recently diagnosed with stage 1-3 breast cancer are assigned to take different types of anti-estrogen and targeted therapy medications to find out how best to shrink male breast cancer before surgery. The results of this trial will advance treatment for male breast cancer patients in the future.
Because breast cancer is less common in males, some patients with male breast cancer can feel isolated or even ashamed of having a cancer typically associated with females. That's why it's important for men to talk with their healthcare team about how they're feeling and, if possible, connect with other male breast cancer survivors in person or through online support groups.
To diagnose more men before their cancers grow large and spread, it's important that they seek medical attention for changes in their chest wall, nipple, underarms or neck. In addition, men who are diagnosed with breast cancer are encouraged to participate in clinical trials, when available, to help improve male breast cancer treatment. Detecting cancer early and optimizing evidence-based treatments will lead to more cures.
Kathryn Ruddy, M.D., Oncology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota

DEAR MAYO CLINIC: My mother was recently diagnosed with breast cancer. Given my family history, when should I consider preventive surgical options, and what do those look like? Are there other risk factors I should be aware of?
ANSWER: Given your family history, it's understandable to think proactively about your breast cancer risk. The good news is that today we have more tools than ever to help people understand their personal risk and choose prevention strategies that fit their goals, health needs and stage of life.
An important first step is meeting with a healthcare clinician experienced in breast cancer risk assessment, such as a breast health specialist at a high-risk breast clinic. Clinicians use a combination of personal history, family history, genetic testing and validated risk-prediction models to estimate your lifetime risk of developing breast cancer.
What factors increase breast cancer risk?
Risk factors may include:
Age.
Genetic mutations, such as BRCA 1 or BRCA 2.
Family history of breast or ovarian cancer.
Hormonal factors, including age at first menstrual period, pregnancy history and breastfeeding.
Prior breast biopsies or certain benign breast conditions.
Breast density on imaging.
Reviewing risk, family history and any genetic results of family members with a genetic counselor may be helpful to determine whether genetic testing may be appropriate for you.
Once your risk is better defined, your care team can recommend a personalized screening plan. For people at higher risk, this may include earlier and more frequent screening, often using breast MRI or other imaging options in addition to mammography.
What are the options for reducing breast cancer risk?
Prevention strategies generally fall into three categories:
Lifestyle approaches. Maintaining a healthy weight, staying physically active, limiting alcohol intake and avoiding smoking can help reduce breast cancer risk. Research shows that combining regular aerobic exercise with strength training offers the most significant benefit.
Risk-reducing medications. Certain medications can lower breast cancer risk by about 50%-70% in select people. These are typically taken daily for several years and may be an option depending on your age, menopausal status and individual risk profile.
Risk-reducing surgery. For some people at very high risk, including those with BRCA mutations, preventive surgery may be considered. A bilateral (double) mastectomy can reduce the risk of developing breast cancer by approximately 90%-95%, although no surgery can eliminate risk entirely. This is a permanent decision that affects appearance, sensation and quality of life, so it’s essential to carefully discuss this with your care team.
When should preventive mastectomy be considered?
Risk-reducing mastectomy can be performed with or without breast reconstruction. There are different approaches to both mastectomy and reconstruction, and eligibility for a particular approach will be discussed by your care team. Options include:
Total mastectomy, which removes the breast tissue and results in a flat chest wall.
Skin-sparing mastectomy, which preserves most of the breast skin.
Nipple-sparing mastectomy, which preserves the skin and nipple-areola complex for select patients.
Robotic-assisted nipple-sparing mastectomy can also be an option for select patients with increased risk of breast cancer who are considering a prophylactic (preventive) mastectomy. This approach also may be used for patients who have early-stage breast cancer with tumors located away from the nipple and skin.
The minimally invasive approach allows the surgeon to remove breast tissue through a small incision near the side of the breast under the arm while preserving the skin and nipple-areola complex. Early experience suggests this technique may reduce visible scarring, improve cosmetic outcomes and improve patient-reported outcomes, such as postoperative physical well-being, while maintaining the same cancer-control principles as other surgical options.
Ongoing evaluation and research continue to refine patient selection and outcomes for this innovative technique.
How do you decide which prevention option is right for you?
Choosing whether, and when, to pursue medication or surgery to reduce breast cancer risk is a deeply personal decision. It also can change over time as circumstances evolve. Factors such as age, menopausal status, plans for pregnancy, family responsibilities and personal values all matter.
Meeting with a breast surgical oncologist, genetic counselor and reconstructive plastic surgeon can help you fully understand your options and feel confident in your decision.
Being proactive about your health is an important step. With individualized care and a thoughtful approach, you and your healthcare team can develop a plan that best supports your long-term well-being.
Jeffrey E. Johnson, M.D., Breast and Melanoma Surgical Oncology, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota, and Mara Piltin, D.O., Surgical Oncology, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, Florida

ROCHESTER, Minn. — Researchers in a Mayo Clinic-led study have shown how to detect a broad range of DNA mutations in noncancerous human tissues and across the genome. The analysis, drawing on more than 90 trillion DNA letters of sequencing data, could help scientists study when these changes arise — from early development through aging — and how they contribute to cancer and other diseases.
Published in Cell, the study is the flagship paper in a package of roughly a dozen publications from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Common Fund's Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues, or SMaHT, Network. The network includes more than 300 members from more than two dozen U.S. universities and hospitals. Researchers evaluated approaches for detecting somatic mutations ranging from single-letter DNA changes to large deletions, insertions and rearrangements.
Alexej Abyzov, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic professor of biomedical informatics who leads the Somatic Mutations in Development and Aging Laboratory, is the corresponding author of the Cell study.
"We often think of the human genome as a single, fixed sequence, but every person is a mosaic of cells that acquire genetic changes over time," Dr. Abyzov says. "As we have increasingly recognized in recent years, these mutations are relevant not only to cancer but also to a broad range of age-related diseases."
Reading the cellular mosaic
Unlike inherited genetic changes, somatic mutations arise after conception and accumulate over a lifetime. As cells divide, they can pass those changes to new cells, creating genetic differences within the same person, known as somatic mosaicism. Some somatic mutations can alter how cells behave and contribute to cancer, aging, and neurodevelopmental, cardiovascular and autoimmune diseases.
These mutations can be difficult to detect when they are rare or occur in complex, repetitive regions of the genome. The SMaHT Network compared short- and long-read whole-genome sequencing, duplex sequencing, single-cell sequencing, and computational approaches.
This illustration shows examples of DNA mutations.
One of the clearest findings came from long-read sequencing, which reads longer stretches of DNA at a time. Much like reading a full sentence instead of a few scattered words, the added context made large genetic changes easier to find. Long-read sequencing detected about twice as many large DNA changes as short-read sequencing. It also found insertions that shorter reads often missed.
Researchers improved detection in other hard-to-read parts of the genome too. In one benchmark, a more complete genome reference raised precision from 79% to 89%. Single-cell sequencing of 102 lung and colon cells revealed differences from cell to cell and helped trace their history back to early development.
Companion study maps rare mutations across tissues
Dr. Abyzov also co-led a companion SMaHT paper published in The American Journal of Human Genetics. Deep whole-genome sequencing accurately detected rare, single-letter DNA changes present at levels below 1% in a tissue sample.
Alexej Abyzov, Ph.D.
Analyzing DNA from different organs also helped detect mutations that arose early in development and spread to multiple tissues. Combining lung and colon data uncovered 13 additional shared mutations, improving detection by 145% for these very rare mutations compared with analyzing either tissue alone.
SMaHT aims to catalog somatic mutations across 10 to 15 tissue types from 150 donors while improving the tools used to detect them. NIH is planning a second stage focused on understanding how these mutations influence biological processes and disease.
Dr. Abyzov says the research could eventually help identify people at higher cancer risk and track precancerous changes in tissues before developing symptoms.
The studies were supported by the NIH Common Fund through the Office of Strategic Coordination in the NIH Office of the Director. The companion study received additional NIH support for work conducted at Mayo Clinic. For complete author lists, disclosures and funding information, review the Cell study and the companion The American Journal of Human Genetics study.

October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month
ROCHESTER, Minnesota — You probably know that a lump in the breast may be a symptom of breast cancer. But what about breast cancer that develops without that warning sign? Inflammatory breast cancer is a fast-moving cancer that doesn't usually form a lump; instead, the skin on one breast changes rapidly, explains Tina Hieken, M.D., a surgical oncologist at Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center.
Inflammatory breast cancer often comes with symptoms that mimic inflammation of the breast, such as a change in skin color to a pink, red, purple or bruised appearance, unusual warmth in the affected breast, and orange peel-like skin, a symptom known as peau d'orange.
As a result, inflammatory breast cancers may be misdiagnosed as cellulitis, mastitis, Paget’s disease of the breast, or other more benign conditions.
Inflammatory breast cancer accounts for roughly 1% to 5% of breast cancer diagnoses but 10% of breast cancer deaths, statistics show.
"When there are changes in the skin of the breast, particularly in women who aren't nursing and do not have breastfeeding-associated redness, that can be a warning sign of cancer and should be evaluated by a medical professional," Dr. Hieken says.
"In inflammatory breast cancer, symptoms can develop within a few months," she notes. "That's different from someone noting a lump in the breast over a period of time, and then secondarily, skin changes in the breast over a year or longer."
In inflammatory breast cancer, abnormal cells go through the lymphatic channels in skin and soft tissue, accounting for the skin changes in the breast, Dr. Hieken explains.
Inflammatory breast cancer treatment
Inflammatory breast cancer is treated first with systemic therapy: a treatment that goes through the whole body, she says. That therapy is based on the cancer's biological features, or subtype, such as whether it expresses the estrogen receptor or overexpresses the HER2 protein.
The systemic therapy is usually delivered intravenously and could be:
Chemotherapy directed at rapidly dividing cells.
Targeted therapy aimed at cells that overexpress the HER2 protein.
Immunotherapy to help the body fight cancer that doesn't express the estrogen receptor or the HER2 protein; this is the least common type, Dr. Hieken says.
Then, surgery includes removal of the breast and nearby lymph nodes, typically followed by radiation that includes the chest, armpit and shoulder. This three-mode approach of whole-body therapy, surgery and radiation is critical to disease control for cancer that has a high risk of spreading to other parts of the body or recurring in the breast and surrounding area, Dr. Hieken says. More common forms of breast cancer may not require all types of available treatments.
Advances in inflammatory breast cancer care
There have been several innovations in the treatment of inflammatory breast cancer.
"Very similar to non-inflammatory breast cancer, giving treatment at the beginning that is designed for one of those three or four subtypes of breast cancer is probably the biggest innovation," Dr. Hieken says. "I think in parallel, the other big innovation is better cross-sectional imaging so that, at the outset, we know whether patients have disease that has spread beyond the breast and the regional lymph nodes."
Among the breast cancer subtypes, progress has particularly been made in HER2-positive inflammatory breast cancer, with the addition of two different drugs that work in a complementary way to block the effects of the HER2 protein overexpression, she adds.
"It's been a huge advantage and has really improved outcomes for women," Dr. Hieken says. "Then, for those women who have less than a complete response to that systemic treatment, there are new targeted therapies that can be given after surgery."
Another improvement is intensity modulated radiotherapy, or IMRT, that is delivered using CT integrated planning, she says. This allows the care team to look at a patient in three dimensions and determine how to personalize radiation therapy to minimize the effects through such techniques as having the patient practice breath-holding or lie on her stomach during radiation therapy.
"We're learning a lot," Dr. Hieken adds.
A team approach to inflammatory breast cancer treatment
At Mayo Clinic, physicians from across treatment disciplines work alongside researchers seeking new care options for patients with this aggressive form of cancer.
Specialists from medical oncology, radiation oncology, surgical oncology and radiology work together. They collaborate with additional healthcare professionals such as genetic counselers, pathologists, social workers, occupational and physical therapists, psychotherapists, and integrative medicine experts, to offer comprehensive support to patients.
For more information about inflammatory breast cancer, visit mayoclinic.org and the Mayo Clinic Medical Professionals website.
